detail.abstract: This article introduces and explores the concept of "architectural advertising" as a strategic tool in luxury branding. In an era of globalized competition, architecture transcends its functional role to become a primary medium for transmitting brand values and shaping consumer experiences. This study argues that flagship stores of luxury brands operate as cultural symbols that significantly influence urban identity. Through a multi-method qualitative analysis of cases like Dior (Paris), Balenciaga (New York), and Tommy Hilfiger (London), we demonstrate how architectural design promotes specific consumer behaviors and cultural patterns. Furthermore, the article introduces the novel concept of "advertising migration," elucidating how brand architecture attracts flows of people to urban centers, thereby altering socio-cultural dynamics. Our findings reveal a tension between the homogenizing force of global brand identities and the preservation of local cultural authenticity.

title: Brand Premium: Evidence from Asia
affiliations: Sabanci University, Sabanci University Graduate School of Management, Sabanci University and Sabanci University

detail.title: Brand Premium: Evidence from Asia
detail.abstract: This paper examines the relation between brand values and the cross-section of equity returns in China, Japan and Korea. Using Interbrand's best brand lists for each local market, we find that a value-weighted portfolio of stocks with top brands generates an annual abnormal return of 6-10%. This result is robust to alternative portfolio weighting schemes and the inclusion of intangibilityrelated factors in the pricing models. Moreover, the inclusion and exclusion of top brands in the updated lists enhances the magnitude of the brand premium. Cross-sectional regressions that control for a variety of firm characteristics including intangible ones reiterate the finding that stocks with highly valuable brands exhibit outperformance. These results are consistent with the hypothesis that market participants underestimate the value of brands when they perform company valuations.

detail.abstract: We study creative marketplaces where consumers can either purchase human-created content or produce content using a platform-integrated generative artificial intelligence (AI) system. The quality and required prompting effort of the AI system depend on its fine-tuning data, which creators may contribute to voluntarily in exchange for compensation. Integrating generative AI increases platform profits by unlocking demand from mismatched consumers, and it may be optimal for the platform to charge a higher price for AI-generated content than for human created content. This AI price premium increases with the steerability of the underlying generative AI model. When creators are compensated for contributing to the fine-tuning data, a creator displaced by AI can be strictly better off shifting from producing content for humans to supplying training data for AI. Our results show how platform design shapes the distribution of profits and welfare when creators train the AI that may replace them, offering guidance for the design and governance of efficient and equitable creative markets in the age of AI.

title: Instant Gratification: The Quick Commerce Phenomenon in India

detail.title: Instant Gratification: The Quick Commerce Phenomenon in India
detail.abstract: The case study explores the transformative impact of quick commerce on the Indian retail landscape, highlighting its rapid evolution and the competitive dynamics among key players. As the market for quick commerce expands, driven by changing consumer preferences for speed and convenience, companies like Zepto, Blinkit, and Swiggy Instamart are redefining the online shopping experience by promising delivery within minutes. This study examines the innovative business models adopted by these companies, including the use of dark stores and partnerships with local retailers, which enable them to meet the growing demand for instant delivery. Additionally, it analyzes the significant growth trajectory of the quickcommerce sector, which has outpaced traditional e-commerce, and discusses the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead, including technological advancements, sustainability concerns, and evolving consumer behaviors. With India poised to become one of the largest economies globally, this case study provides valuable insights into the future of retail in the country and the critical role that quick commerce will play in shaping consumer experiences and market dynamics.

title: Can Collective Action Campaigns Drive Dietary Change? Evidence from the Netherlands
affiliations: Tilburg University, Tilburg University - Tilburg University School of Economics and Management and Tilburg University, CentER

detail.title: Can Collective Action Campaigns Drive Dietary Change? Evidence from the Netherlands
detail.abstract: Since 2018, major food retailers, manufacturers, NGOs, and consumer organizations in the Netherlands have jointly organized a nationwide campaign encouraging consumers to abstain from animal-based foods for one week each year. The campaign spans all major media channels and virtually every retail store, achieving a share of voice and geographic reach comparable to large-scale marketing initiatives. Using household scanner data and a border-based difference-indifferences design comparing the Netherlands with Germany, we find that the campaign produces a substantial short-term increase in the purchase share of plant-based meat alternatives but does not substantially reduce animal-meat purchases. The 10-week cumulative effect is 2.60 percentage points, only marginally larger than the immediate effect. Its impact is therefore large but transient, dissipating quickly after the campaign period.

title: Maximizing Reach and Efficiency of Digital Out-of-Home Advertising
affiliations: , Northeastern University - D'Amore-McKim School of Business and

detail.title: Maximizing Reach and Efficiency of Digital Out-of-Home Advertising
detail.abstract: Digital transformation can offer firms benefits, yet often requires substantial upfront investment. This research investigates the returns to digital transformation in the out-of-home (OOH) advertising industry by quantifying the causal impact of digital billboards on consumer behavior. Leveraging a field experiment conducted with a digital OOH (DOOH) advertising platform, we estimate the incremental effect of ad exposure on website visitation and explore the dynamics of repeated exposures, including wear-in and wear-out effects. The frequent, exogenously timed ad rotations inherent to DOOH enable us to exploit random consumer arrival as a source of experimental variation. We find that exposure to the digital billboard ad significantly increases and accelerates visitation to the advertiser’s website. However, we also observe diminishing returns and signs of weariness of repeated exposures, highlighting the importance of optimizing ad intensity. A simulation analysis further demonstrates that DOOH is substantially more efficient than traditional OOH, primarily due to its ability to dynamically control ad delivery, reduce overexposure, and maintain high reach. These findings offer empirical evidence supporting the effectiveness of digital billboards and broader implications for evaluating the ROI of marketing-related digital transformation.

title: Leveraging Data for Competitive Advantage: Toward a Data-Based View of the Firm

detail.title: Leveraging Data for Competitive Advantage: Toward a Data-Based View of the Firm
detail.abstract: This study introduces the Data-Based View (DBV) as a novel framework for understanding firm growth in the era of data and digital intelligence. The DBV explains how organizations can create and sustain competitive advantages by leveraging both internal and external data resources. The framework is built on four key attributes of data utilization: context-dependency, data as a generic input, abstract representation, and inherent objectivity. Furthermore, the study identifies four empirical indicators of valuable data: accuracy, relevance, benchmarkability, and extractability. Central to the DBV are two core capabilities—value-generating and value-safeguarding—which together enable firms to enhance customer insights, drive innovation, and improve operational efficiency. The paper concludes by discussing the applicability of the DBV, outlining the conditions under which it is most effective and its broader implications for organizational strategy.

title: Sponsored Search with AI-Generated Ad Content
affiliations: The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) - Department of Information Systems, Business Statistics and Operations Management, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen -School of Data Science and University of Western Ontario - Ivey Business School

detail.title: Sponsored Search with AI-Generated Ad Content
detail.abstract: Sponsored search has long been the dominant mechanism in online advertising, allowing platforms to monetize high-traffic ad positions through competitive bidding. Traditionally, advertisers retained control over ad content, while platforms managed ad position allocation and pricing. Recent advances in generative AI are reshaping this paradigm by enabling platforms to generate and control ad content directly. This shift raises a fundamental question: how should platforms leverage content control to reconcile the classic trade-off between broad exposure and targeted relevance? We develop a theoretical model of two-position sponsored search with AI-generated ad content, where the platform allocates positions and decides whether each ad is broadly appealing or selectively targeted to matched consumers. We show that platform-controlled content transforms the economics of sponsored search: it enables targeted advertising to enhance-rather than undermine-revenue by managing traffic flow and reducing information rents. Targeting at the top position can strategically redirect unmatched consumers to the lower position, increasing its value. This traffic management effect can even justify placing a lower-margin advertiser in the premium slot-a counterintuitive result that challenges conventional wisdom. At the lower position, targeting serves as an incentive compatibility device, deterring high-margin advertisers from misreporting their type. Our results demonstrate that AI-generated content empowers platforms to unlock new levers of revenue optimization, positioning content design as a tool for strategic control, incentive alignment, and long-term value creation in sponsored search.

detail.abstract: The Mobile Commerce has been exponantially growing, with the rapid usage of smartphones, their advanced functionality through smart features in mobile applications and convenience of buying preferred product/service at any time and any place. The mobile shopping applications have gained a wider acceptance among the Indian consumers in the recent years for many reasons. The purpose of this study is to examine the effects of perceived trust and price saving orientation on customer loyalty and the mediating role of customer satisfaction. Data were collected from 535 current users of mobile shopping applications in India. The PLS-SEM approach was applied to examine the measurement and structural model. Further, the study also aimed to investigate the effects of gender and age on the proposed research model, which was tested through MICOM procedure. The results revealed the significant effects of perceived trust and price saving orientation on customer loyalty, which was also mediated by customer satisfaction. Finally, the effects of gender and age were not statistically significant in the hypothesized relationships of the research model.

title: European Public Goods
affiliations: HEC Paris

detail.title: European Public Goods
detail.abstract: With the EU notoriously struggling to articulate a persuasive narrative, the concept of European Public Goods has recently emerged as reference point for legitimizing centralized EU action. The Draghi report and Letta report both refer to this concept, the contours of which remain vaguely defined. While lawyers have not adopted public goods as a core normative category, this piece examines the legal perspective on European public goods. By applying the criteria of fiscal federalism theory, which includes externalities, economies of scale, and preference homogeneity, the analysis demonstrates that trade-offs occur between these benchmarks depending on the specific public goods in question. The EU institutional and legal framework offers instruments and principles to effectively address this trade-off. This paper considers five levers that allow for the customization of public goods at either EU or Member States level (or both), taking into account the specific characteristics of each. These include the allocation of competences within the margins of the Treaty; the decision-making rules in the Council; the provision of public goods at the level of 'clubs' of member states with similar preferences organized within or outside the Treaty; a variable combination of centralization/decentralization of rulemaking, financing, and delivery of public goods; and compensation or redistributive mechanisms to achieve greater alignment of preferences. One of the principal implications of the legal contribution to the discourse on European public goods is that the question of whether public goods should be provided at the national or European level may be a misguided one. The pertinent question, therefore, is how to establish institutional frameworks for the provision of public goods, with a view to optimising the benefits of such goods for EU members.

detail.title: C-Suite in the Crosshairs:  The Rising Tide of Individual Civil and Criminal Accountability for Executives [Bloomberg Law - Forthcoming]
detail.abstract:
This article explores the growing erosion of the boundary between corporate and personal liability. Delaware’s landmark In re McDonald’s Corp. Stockholder Derivative Litigation (2023) extended Caremark-style oversight duties to corporate officers, exposing executives to personal derivative claims for failing to act on compliance or risk warnings. Federal authorities have likewise renewed their focus on individual accountability, with DOJ and SEC policies emphasizing prosecution of responsible executives under the FCPA and Section 20(a) “control-person” liability.

The authors also examine new areas of exposure (including ESG disclosures, supply-chain transparency, and AI governance) where regulators expect active oversight. To mitigate risk, companies should clarify executive responsibilities, formalize escalation protocols, and strengthen D&O coverage. 

The article concludes that effective oversight and documentation are now essential forms of self-protection.

detail.abstract: Healthcare and public sector organizations face unique and complex challenges in managing human capital due to stringent regulatory oversight and a growing demand for services. Traditional HR systems in these sectors are often fragmented and incapable of supporting modern requirements for transparency, agility, and strategic workforce planning. This article examines the modernization of HR practices in these regulated contexts through the adoption of cloud-based Human Capital Management (HCM) solutions. Drawing from academic literature, industry case studies, and thirdparty analyst reports, this paper analyzes how Oracle HCM Cloud can enhance compliance, strengthen data governance, and drive operational efficiency. It presents case examples to illustrate measurable impacts in areas such as credentialing, audit readiness, and workforce scheduling. Ethical considerations surrounding privacy, algorithmic fairness, and public trust are also explored. This analysis suggests that these modernization initiatives are critical for guiding HR transformation at the intersection of technology, regulation, and human capital strategy.

detail.abstract: Businesses increasingly rely on middleware to enable seamless data movement across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. However, traditional integration systems remain reactive and lack predictive capabilities. This study introduces an AI-enhanced middleware framework that fuses real-time telemetry, machine learning, and adaptive policy control to anticipate and mitigate problems before they affect operations. The proposed multilayer architecture predicts latency, detects anomalies, and dynamically adjusts routing to maintain resilience and compliance at scale. Empirical validation across retail, logistics, finance, and healthcare scenarios demonstrates reductions of up to 35-55 percent in recovery time and 40 percent faster issue resolution. The framework highlights the importance of governance, explainable AI, and cross-functional collaboration, showing that predictive middleware can transform integration from passive connectivity into intelligent enterprise infrastructure.

detail.title:
The Legality of Omnibus Legislation Under EU Law:
A Preliminary Analysis of Omnibus I Simplification Directive of CSRD and CSDD and its Legal Consequences on the EU Legal Order
detail.abstract: This paper provides a preliminary analysis of the legal issues arising from the European Union's use of the Omnibus as the privileged legislative technique to 'simplify' its existing regulatory framework. While the EU has used this method occasionally, it was traditionally reserved for technical consolidation. Therefore, the EU's novel deployment of omnibus legislation to 'simplify' its rules, by substantively amending existing legislation across multiple domains, represents a fundamental departure from established EU lawmaking that raises serious questions of legality. The shift is not merely one of scale but of constitutional function: the Omnibus has migrated from being an occasional administrative convenience to becoming the preferred vehicle for implementing a comprehensive deregulatory agenda while bypassing procedural integrity. Using the proposed Omnibus Simplification Directive (amending the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive-CSRD and Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive-CSDDD) as the primary case study, this memorandum argues that while omnibus legislation is not per se incompatible with EU law, its deployment as a systematic mechanism to pursue its simplification agenda conflicts with EU core constitutional principles. The Omnibus I exemplifies this conclusion insofar as its Simplification Directive's proposal violates the principle of proportionality under Article 5(4) TEU and undermines the constitutional architecture of evidence-based, participatory lawmaking enshrined in Article 11 TEU and Article 296 TFEU. As the EU prepares more Omnibus packages, the question of whether this failure represents an isolated deviation subject to correction or the inauguration of a new constitutional normal characterized by constitutional drift remains to be determined. That determination lies not with legal analysis but with political choice, a choice the EU legislature must now make, mindfully and deliberately, understanding that its implications will extend far beyond the immediate measures under consideration. To remedy such a risk, this paper suggests constraining the use of the Omnibus within the boundaries of a dedicated regime, aimed at ensuring its compatibility with the EU legal order.

title: How Game Designers Disguise Gambling as Gaming: The Gacha Addiction Cycle
affiliations: Chalmers University of Technology, Chalmers University of Technology and University of Gothenburg

detail.title: How Game Designers Disguise Gambling as Gaming: The Gacha Addiction Cycle
detail.abstract: This study examines how gacha games sustain player retention through an interaction of design mechanics, psychological responses, and social dynamics. Using a qualitative, secondary-research approach, we synthesize literature and case evidence across East Asian gacha titles and Western games that implement analogous systems (e.g., rotating shops and battle passes). We find that retention is driven by four mutually reinforcing levers: (i) engineered scarcity and limited-time windows that induce fear of missing out and schedule-bound return; (ii) variable-reward structures and near-miss effects buffered by 'pity' guarantees, which cognitively reframe losses as progress toward an inevitable win; (iii) habit scaffolding via daily/weekly tasks and energy gates that normalize lightweight, high-frequency engagement; and (iv) a social amplifier that converts rare acquisitions into visible status signals, heightening anticipation before pulls and conferring prestige after success. This research could deepen the understanding of the tight relationship between gacha games and their communities, which would be useful to form stronger connections between them and player behavior.

title: Resalable Bytes: Unlocking Digital Ownership in Content Markets through Blockchain
affiliations: Texas Tech University - Rawls College of Business, University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management and University of Washington - Michael G. Foster School of Business

detail.title: Resalable Bytes: Unlocking Digital Ownership in Content Markets through Blockchain
detail.abstract: Tokenization has emerged as a transformative blockchain application that converts illiquid real-world and digital assets into verifiable tokens, enabling ownership transfer and unlocking new sources of value. We develop a game-theoretic model to examine how tokenization reshapes digital content markets by facilitating blockchain-based ownership and resale. We compare a benchmark without true consumer ownership to two implementation models: creator-initiated blockchain (CIB) and platform-initiated blockchain (PIB). Our analysis yields important insights. CIB and PIB operate through distinct mechanisms that generate different market outcomes. Under CIB, welfare gains arise from both resale effect and competition effect, as the creator’s blockchain channel competes with the platform’s traditional one, reducing prices and broadening market participation. Under PIB, resale occurs within the platform’s own channel, and welfare gains depend primarily on the resale effect, which must outweigh the higher prices charged by the platform. The value of tokenization further depends on the blockchain’s operational efficiency and consumer adoption, affected by the initiator-side operating costs and consumer’s resale costs, respectively. Finally, adoption incentives are asymmetric. Creators embrace blockchain more readily as CIB grants them direct access to consumers, while platforms adopt blockchain cautiously. Nevertheless, a forward-looking platform may adopt blockchain defensively to preempt creator entry.

It explores the surge in demand for electric scooters as sustainable alternatives to traditional vehicles, driven by environmental concerns and government policies. The study examines the growth, challenges, and strategies within the electric scooters market, highlighting technological advancements, consumer behavior, marketing strategies, and the crucial role of charging infrastructure. With a focus on the competitive landscape, industry challenges, and the potential for widespread adoption, the case study underscores the pivotal role of electric scooters in shaping a cleaner, more sustainable future for urban transportation in India.

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming

detail.abstract: We study how U.S. retirees draw down nonhousing financial assets using longitudinal data from the Health and Retirement Study (1995 to 2020). While life-cycle models predict gradual decumulation to support consumption, we find many retirees retain substantial wealth into later life. IRA balances decline steadily, consistent with required minimum distribution rules. Brokerage holdings are decumulated more quickly, especially among middle-wealth households. In contrast, checking and savings balances remain stable. Financial literacy is strongly associated with slower decumulation, higher asset levels, and reduced debt. These patterns suggest that asset type, institutional rules, and individual capabilities jointly shape financial outcomes in retirement.

title: Macro-trends Impacting the Evolution of Higher Education
affiliations: TIAA Institute

detail.title: Macro-trends Impacting the Evolution of Higher Education

publicationDetails.detailsText: TIAA Institute Research Paper Series Forthcoming

detail.abstract:
For generations of Americans, higher education has stood as a beacon of personal achievement and a clear path to a better life. The role of colleges and universities in delivering on that promise has long been regarded as self-evident. In 1973, Derek C. Bok, barely two years into his tenure as president of Harvard University, declared with confidence that the fundamental purpose of a college education “scarcely requires justification.” 

A half-century later, evidence suggests the value of a college degree, and the reasons for pursuing one, are as important as ever. Yet a combination of forces is putting this long-term perspective to the test. While colleges and universities continue to attract millions of students each year and many elite institutions are flooded with applications, the higher education system overall is grappling with challenges ranging from rising costs and shifting demographics to technological change and eroding public support.

If the challenges are great, so is the opportunity. Higher education can and should remain a vital force in shaping individual lives, leveling the field of opportunity for all Americans and preparing new generations to propel society forward. This report examines several macro-trends creating headwinds for higher education today, as well as some popular misperceptions that, left unanswered, may place the future viability of many institutions at risk. We conclude with some ideas on how individual colleges and universities, and the higher education community as a whole, can adapt to remain a critical component of the American economy through the 21st century.

title: Understanding the factors behind (and boosting) basic and functional literacy rates in the Philippines
affiliations: Ateneo De Manila University - Ateneo School of Government, Department of Education and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Understanding the factors behind (and boosting) basic and functional literacy rates in the Philippines
detail.abstract: Every five (5) years, the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) conducts a Functional Literacy, Education, and Mass Media Survey (FLEMMS), and the latest data (based on a survey conducted in September-October 2024) was released last 4 April 2025. The findings require a more nuanced analysis, given this recent data release involves a redefinition in both the basic and functional literacy rate calculations. This note clarifies that the country’s literacy indicators under both the old and new definitions have been following an upward trajectory. Nevertheless, the recalibrated definitions for both basic and functional literacy have raised the bar on both fronts, leading to relatively lower headline indicators for both basic and functional literacy. More importantly, the gap between basic and functional literacy has increased under the new (more stringent) definition of functional literacy which now emphasizes comprehension of written text, in addition to skills in reading, writing and computing. This note briefly reviews the relevant evidence on ways to boost comprehension skills, as well as potential factors influencing the gap between basic and functional literacy. It also reviews the Department of Education’s (DepEd’s) policies and programs to barrow this literacy gap; and it concludes by outlining the DepEd’s strategic plan on sustaining reforms to boost literacy, notably through technology.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between operational sustainability expenditure and firm value using a sample of firms from 38 countries. We find that operational sustainability expenditure is positively associated with firm value. This finding suggests that investors positively evaluate firmlevel expenditure on operational sustainability activities. We also document that the presence of a sustainability committee, stakeholder engagement and eco-innovation, and the inclusion of sustainability-related targets in compensation contracts of Chief Executive Officers (CEOs) positively moderate the association between operational sustainability expenditure and firm value. Additionally, country-level factors, such as strong governance, a stakeholder-oriented business culture and investor protection, as well as firms that operate in environmentally sensitive industries further enhance this relationship. These findings have important implications for regulators, policymakers, investors and other stakeholders, highlighting the value of strategic operational sustainability expenditure. Specifically, regulators can use these findings to better understand the importance of adopting tangible and monetary measures when evaluating firms' commitment to operational sustainability.

title: The Legal and Financial Intersection of ESG-Driven Investments
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Legal and Financial Intersection of ESG-Driven Investments
detail.abstract: ESG-driven investment blends environmental, social and governance criteria with finance, intertwining regulatory duties and market forces. Legally, UK firms face mandatory climate reporting (TCFD-aligned disclosures under FCA listing rules) and evolving governance codes requiring sustainability oversight. Regulatory bodies (HM Treasury, FCA, FRC) are establishing frameworks: for example, the FCA's new Sustainable Disclosure Regime (SDR) imposes an anti-greenwashing rule and ESG fund labelling. Treasury has also prioritized transition planning over a formal taxonomy. Financially, evidence shows that robust ESG integration can enhance firm value and reduce risk. For instance, strong ESG practices tend to lower the cost of capital and improve investor confidence, as academic studies on UK firms suggest. However, balancing long-term ESG goals with fiduciary duty and avoiding misleading claims remains a key challenge. This section explores the complex interplay between ESG regulation, corporate governance and investment outcomes.

title: Migration Shocks as Labor Supply Constraints: The Inflationary Consequences of Restricted Workforce Flows
affiliations: University of Texas at El Paso - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: Migration Shocks as Labor Supply Constraints: The Inflationary Consequences of Restricted Workforce Flows
detail.abstract: Labor shortages can drive inflationary pressures by increasing production costs and limiting firms' ability to meet the demand for goods and services. Focusing on pandemic-related visa restrictions as a natural experiment, this paper examines the impact of labor supply disruptions on inflation across metropolitan areas and industries in the US. The analysis constructs a city-industry-level measure of exposure to labor supply shocks based on baseline reliance on foreign-born workers and variation in visa restrictions by country of origin. Using a difference-in-differences framework, the analysis finds that metropolitan areas and sectors more exposed to labor supply disruptions experienced greater inflationary pressures. The results, which are not driven by pre-existing trends, suggest that restricted labor mobility contributed to rising prices in the post-pandemic recovery through increased labor market tightness. These findings provide new evidence on the inflationary consequences of labor supply shocks and highlight the macroeconomic importance of migration as a stabilizing force in labor markets.

title: Balancing Innovation and Investor Protection in FinTech Frameworks
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Balancing Innovation and Investor Protection in FinTech Frameworks
detail.abstract: The UK FinTech sector is globally prominent, driven by technologies like open banking, AI, blockchain and digital payments. Regulators therefore strive to nurture innovation while safeguarding consumers. On the innovation side, the FCA's Regulatory Sandbox and Innovation Hub provide controlled environments to test new services, reducing time-to-market. Government support (via "API first" open banking mandates and digital licensing) further accelerates new entrants. Conversely, investor protection is assured through existing rules: fintech firms must obtain FCA/PRA authorisation and comply with financial promotion, AML/KYC and data security laws. Recent FCA initiatives exemplify this balance: for instance, proposals to lift the retail ban on crypto ETNs impose strict listing and disclosure requirements. Overall, UK law employs a principles-based approach, using tailored regulatory sandboxes and updated rules (like the Consumer Duty) to allow creative financial services to flourish in a safe, well regulated environment.

detail.title: The Valuation of Certificates of Deposits
detail.abstract: Bank certificates of deposit (CDs) allow investors to secure a fixed interest rate over a specified term. Some CD products also include embedded option features-for example, Rate Bump CDs give consumers the right to increase their rate once or more during the contract term. Using an arbitrage free pricing framework, we show that CDs are frequently mispriced relative to both the U.S. Treasury market and the banks' own competing CD offerings. Interestingly, the mispricing does not always favor banks. While banks have full control over setting CD rates, consumers can at times earn returns above the market without taking on additional risk.

title: Towards stronger learning outcomes under decentralization, digitalization and public-private partnerships: Reform prospects in the Philippines' basic education sector
affiliations: Ateneo De Manila University - Ateneo School of Government, Department of Education, Republic of the Philippines and Department of Education

detail.title: Towards stronger learning outcomes under decentralization, digitalization and public-private partnerships: Reform prospects in the Philippines' basic education sector
detail.abstract: Reforming the basic education system is a herculean task that has lingered for the last several decades. Congested classrooms, inadequate teacher training, delayed delivery of textbooks and other key learning materials, inadequate innovation and overcentralized decision making are only some of the main challenges that have festered, debilitating education quality in the Philippines for years now. In order to modernize and improve the quality of the Philippine basic education system, ongoing reforms pursued by the Department of Education (DepEd) focus on two main areas. The first involves ramping up and frontloading investments in education so that they meet international benchmarks and better match the urgency from the country’s rapidly closing demographic dividend. The second area tries to improve the governance of these resources and the system as a whole, by pivoting towards decentralization, transparency, evaluations (and learning) and partnerships. There is an urgency to this reform and investment task in basic education—analysis suggests that every additional dollar the Philippine government spends on school-age children yields a return of USD 2.3 flowing back into the economy. These findings emphasize how inaction and underinvestment likely consign millions to low-income status, and also likely debilitate the country’s economic development and growth prospects. This paper outlines the main reforms and urgent actions pursued by reformists in the Department of Education.

title: Toward A Normative Framework For A Payment Stablecoin Financial Market Infrastructure

detail.title: Toward A Normative Framework For A Payment Stablecoin Financial Market Infrastructure
detail.abstract:
Stablecoins, a type of privately issued digital money, have the potential to become a mainstream payment instrument and support the growth of the digital economy, yet several challenges hinder their widespread adoption.

This paper examines whether risk management tools utilized by settlement systems, clearing houses and other financial markets infrastructures (FMIs), can be leveraged to overcome the current obstacles to stablecoins becoming a mainstream payment instrument. The goal is to safeguard systemic stability and consumer protection, without reneging on the decentralized attribute of digital finance at the peer-to-peer payment level, in a market that is projected to grow to between $500 million and $2 trillion in the coming years.

Current obstacles to the adoption of payment stablecoins include: a lack of singleness of money; challenges with interoperability; a fragmented many to many network; counterparty risk; settlement risk; a lack of elastic liquidity; a lack of market integrity.

Currently, there is no clearing house for payment stablecoins. The Silvergate Exchange Network (SEN) was an infrastructure designed for the digital economy, but unlike a clearing house or settlement system that relies on the financial support of a group of members, SEN depended on the support of one financial institution, and when that financial institution failed, SEN also failed. This paper also examines key provisions of the GENIUS Act, as well as analogies and differences between payment stablecoins, foreign exchange, and money market mutual funds.

There is an inverse relationship between speed of settlement and liquidity risk. Netting and portfolio compression can reduce liquidity risk, while the near-instantaneous settlement of blockchain native stablecoins can reduce settlement risk. This paper sets out possible frameworks for a payment stablecoin FMI as a self-regulated industry utility, or an entity subject to regulatory oversight.

title: Glass-Substrate UCIe 3.0 Heterogeneous EV Power-Control Module with RISC-V Safety Core, GaN Point-of-Load PDN Co-Design, and a Packaging Digital Twin
affiliations: NMAM Institute of Technology

detail.title: Glass-Substrate UCIe 3.0 Heterogeneous EV Power-Control Module with RISC-V Safety Core, GaN Point-of-Load PDN Co-Design, and a Packaging Digital Twin
detail.abstract: This paper presents a glass-substrate, chiplet-based EV power-control module that integrates a RISC-V safety microcore, GaN point-of-load regulators, and sensor/gate-driver dice interconnected using UCIe 3.0 with manageability features for power-aware safety and resilience. We develop a packaging digital twin that co-models PDN impedance, thermal fields, and EMI behaviors in embedded-glass, and a compliance and fault-stress harness to validate runtime recalibration, priority sideband transport, and emergency shutdown policies under fast-switching noise typical of SiC/GaN traction and charging environments. Results demonstrate improved link integrity at 48-64 GT/s under EMI stress, reduced transient droop via POL proximity on glass, and higher thermal headroom under tropical ambients representative of Indian operating conditions, while outlining KGD/DFT and yield trade-offs for OSAT ramps. The methodology is standards-aligned, fabrication-free, and targets rapid industrial adoption within India's advanced packaging and EV ecosystem.

title: Enhancing Startup Life Cycle Rigor and Applicability: A Systematic Literature Review and Framework Validation
affiliations: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS) - Department of Industrial Engineering, Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), IESEG School of Management and Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS), Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul (UFRGS)

detail.title: Enhancing Startup Life Cycle Rigor and Applicability: A Systematic Literature Review and Framework Validation

declarations.funderStatement: This study was financed in part by the Coordenação de Aperfeiçoamento de Pessoal de Nível Superior – Brasil (CAPES) – Finance Code 001

detail.abstract: Startups are critical engines of innovation but face high uncertainty and mortality. Existing life cycle models offer limited guidance because they define evolving stages inconsistently and often overlook non-linear trajectories. The aim of this research was to (i) systematically review the startup life cycle literature and (ii) propose and validate an integrative framework for the startup life cycle. This framework clarifies stage boundaries, acknowledges pivots and premature scaling, and enables startup development diagnosis and guidance. It was derived from the systematic analysis of 54 studies, including 29 distinct life cycle models, and validated with 40 experts (20 entrepreneurs and 20 innovation specialists). It was later applied to assess more than 1,300 startups in a public policy initiative in Brazil. The framework contributes theoretically by integrating fragmented approaches into a coherent structure and offering a basis for comparing studies on startup evolution. It also allows examining edge cases such as multi-product ventures and atypical growth paths. From a practical perspective, it helps entrepreneurs allocate resources more effectively, enables accelerators to tailor mentoring and support, and assists policymakers in designing stagespecific interventions. By bridging academic rigor with actionable insights, this research advances knowledge on startup development while improving decision-making in entrepreneurial ecosystems.

title: Macroeconomic Determinants of Unemployment in ECOWAS Countries

detail.title: Macroeconomic Determinants of Unemployment in ECOWAS Countries

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ozili, P.K. (2025). Macroeconomic determinants of unemployment in ECOWAS countries. International Journal of Sustainable Economy, 17(4), 373-396

detail.abstract: Unemployment is a major issue in ECOWAS countries and its determinants are not well-known. We investigate the macroeconomic determinants of unemployment in ECOWAS countries using data from 1993 to 2021. The data were analysed using the panel fixed effect and random effect regression methods. It was found that real GDP growth and central bank asset to GDP ratio are significant macroeconomic determinants of unemployment while inflation rate and domestic private credit have an insignificant effect on unemployment in ECOWAS countries. It was also found that higher domestic private credit significantly decreases unemployment during periods of economic expansion while periods of deflation decrease the rate of unemployment in ECOWAS countries. Positive economic growth is associated with low unemployment in ECOWAS countries.

title: Trends and Patterns of Banking Frauds in Private and Government Banks: A Comparative Analysis (2020
affiliations: KR Mangalam University

detail.title: Trends and Patterns of Banking Frauds in Private and Government Banks: A Comparative Analysis (2020
detail.abstract: In India over the five-year period from 2020 to 2025. Drawing on data from Reserve bank of India (RBI)reports and related literature, the research investigates the incidence, nature, and financial impact of fraud across the two sectors. Findings reveal that private banks report a higher volume of fraud cases, primarily linked to digital payments such as card and internet fraud, which constitute most fraud incidents in terms of frequency. Government banks, however, experience significantly larger fraud amounts, predominantly associated with loan portfolio frauds and advances. The analysis highlights a growing disparity where cases in government banks, though fewer in number, contribute a majority share to the total fraud value. The evolution of fraud typologies indicates an increase in technologically sophisticated schemes in private banks, whereas systemic vulnerabilities in credit appraisal and monitoring largely drive fraud in government banks. The study also evaluates the effectiveness of fraud prevention and detection measures implemented by both sectors, noting a declining trend in fraud cases since 2020 attributed to regulatory reforms, enhanced internal controls, and technology adoption. However, challenges persist, including underreporting, evolving fraud techniques, and the need for sector-specific frameworks. Policy recommendations emphasize strengthening digital security infrastructure in private banks and improving loan monitoring mechanisms in public banks to curb financial losses. This research contributes empirical insights into the dynamic fraud landscape, supporting bankers, regulators, and policymakers in fortifying fraud resilience and protecting the integrity of the Indian banking system.

title: Youth Higher Intensity, Higher Gains?
affiliations: University of Waikato - Management School and The University of Dodoma

detail.title: Youth Higher Intensity, Higher Gains?
detail.abstract: Agriculture and youth are two of the mega topics in the 21st century. Agriculture is essential for livelihoods and economic growth. Youth can drive the sector today and, in the future, if attracted to being involved in it. Their involvement can create jobs and improve farm performance for economic growth. The extant understanding indicates that initiatives have not produced the desirable youth participation in the sector. The impacts of low youth buy-in in agriculture include youth unemployment, food insecurity, and poverty. Further, academic investigations have focused on contextual factors, challenges, attitudes and perceptions, and the impact of training programs to win higher youth buy-in in agriculture. However, studies about the impact of youth intensity of participation in agriculture on farm performance is scanty. Using a nationally representative sample of data from the National Sample Census of Agriculture (NSCA) of 2020, we examined the impact of youth intensity of participation in agriculture on crop yields, net returns, and return on investment (ROI). We adopt a doubly robust IPWRA estimator backed by PSM and ESR models. The average treatment on the treated (ATT) for crop yields, net returns, and return on investment (ROI) is higher for higher-intensity participants. The results suggest that effective interventions promoting youth investment in agriculture are crucial for youth to realize the potential of agriculture.

title: Risk Management in Monetary Policy: A Review with Asset Pricing Implications
affiliations: Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, University College London - Department of Economics and University of Texas at Dallas - Naveen Jindal School of Management

detail.title: Risk Management in Monetary Policy: A Review with Asset Pricing Implications
detail.abstract: We review evidence on how the Fed's risk-management approach manifests in the overall Fed's policy stance and how it affects financial market conditions. We argue that policy stance contains a forward-looking conditional component that has long been an integral part of the Fed's policymaking toolkit.  Asymmetric forward-looking policy tilts - motivated by risk-management considerations and revealed via the Fed's communication - complement and extend beyond the effects of direct policy actions. Going back at least to the early 1990s, the Fed has relied on tilts to not only steer market expectations, but equally importantly, to stabilize risk premia and maintain easy financial conditions. We discuss successes and challenges associated with communication via tilts.

title: Investor Beliefs and Expectation Formation
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Stanford Graduate School of Business, Yale University, New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and Vanguard

detail.title: Investor Beliefs and Expectation Formation
detail.abstract:
This article reviews the literature that uses survey data to study expectation formation among investors. We begin by outlining methods for eliciting investor beliefs and summarizing key empirical patterns documented in recent work. Highlighting the persistent cross-sectional heterogeneity in expectations, we then review evidence on the determinants of beliefs, including a new analysis of belief reactions to the tariff announcement in April 2025. Next, we examine how expectations shape financial decision-making, emphasizing the systematic but muted sensitivity of outcomes to belief changes. We conclude by pointing to promising directions for future research on belief measurement, the determinants of expectations, and their implications for policymakers.

title: Minimum Wages and Informality
affiliations: Princeton University, University College London, Columbia University and Sciences Po

detail.title: Minimum Wages and Informality
detail.abstract:
How do minimum wages affect informality? We study the near-doubling of the real minimum wage from 2000 to 2009 in Brazil, where 46% of the workforce is informal. Using labor force surveys covering the informal sector, we show the minimum wage exhibits near full passthrough to informal employees working in formal firms, about half of all informal employees. The formal-to-informal reallocation elasticity with respect to the formal-wage is small: -0.28. Our findings illustrate how minimum wages can positively affect living standards for workers thought beyond the reach of labor law, a sizable share of the workforce in developing economies.

title: The Global Financial Cycle Meets Global Imbalances

detail.title: The Global Financial Cycle Meets Global Imbalances
detail.abstract: This paper studies the role of global banks in cross-border gross and net capital flows. I propose a tractable multi-country model in which leverage-constrained global banks intermediate funds between local banks with heterogeneous projects. Following a relaxation of their constraint, global banks reallocate more funds, generating a global financial cycle: higher gross capital inflows and outflows in all countries. Countries with higher net external liabilities to global banks experience a larger deterioration in their current account balance-a larger increase in net capital flows-driven by a larger increase in investment, after a leveraging up by global banks. Using a GIV instrument (Gabaix and Koijen 2020), I find that a unit standard deviation increase in the leverage of global banks leads to a lower current account of 0.9% GDP in Portugal, a debtor country, while it leads to a higher current account of 0.2% GDP in Israel, a creditor country on global banks. As such, changes in global banks' leverage also play a role in driving global imbalances.

title: The Roots of the Modern American Presidential Campaign
affiliations: University of Chile and York University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Roots of the Modern American Presidential Campaign
detail.abstract:
Campaign tours have become an essential component of U.S. presidential elections. How and when did they begin? We explore the early history of in-person political campaigning in the United States by reconstructing the first presidential campaign tours from historical newspaper clippings. We analyze the decision to campaign, the determinants of where candidates campaigned, and the outcomes of early in-person campaigns. We document an evolving norm of campaigning. This norm evolved well after the expansion of the railroad network. While a national railroad network was a necessary precondition for campaigning to evolve, our findings point to other factors – such as growing urbanization and the decline of federal patronage machines – playing a more important role in the growth of campaigning. We find evidence that being visited on a campaign tour increased voter turnout in a county. However, we do not find a clear effect of campaign visits of a given candidate on his electoral performance.

title: From Asia, With Skills
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: From Asia, With Skills
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the rise of high-skill migration from Asia to the United States over the past three decades and its consequences for both sending and receiving economies. Between 1990 and 2019, migrants from five Asian countries—India, China, South Korea, Japan, and the Philippines—accounted for over one-third of the growth in US software developers and a quarter of the increase in scientists, engineers, and physicians. Drawing on census microdata, visa records, and administrative sources, I show how US demand for talent in information technology, higher education, and healthcare interacted with Asia’s demographic and educational transformations to generate this migration boom. Policy reforms (notably the H-1B, F-1, and J-1 visa programs) and sectoral shifts—such as the internet revolution, declining public support for universities, and aging-related healthcare demand—created persistent needs for foreign students and workers. Asian economies were uniquely positioned to meet this demand through rapid tertiary expansion, strong STEM institutions, English proficiency, and diaspora networks. These inflows boosted US innovation, entrepreneurship, and service-sector productivity while fostering “brain gain” and “brain circulation” in Asia. Together, these trends reveal how talent flows from Asia have become central to the structure and growth of the modern US economy.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Competition, and Welfare
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence, Competition, and Welfare
detail.abstract:
We study how market power in artificial intelligence (AI) shapes wages and welfare in open-economy general equilibrium by treating AI as a priced, imported factor. Across three models, we separate technical efficiency from the impact of upstream price setting. In a two-traded-goods benchmark, the incidence of AI price changes depends on how sectoral skill intensity changes with AI prices; non-monotone intensity can generate “double harm” for unskilled workers (lower real wage after a large decrease in the price of AI, and real wage decreases further when the AI price rises as a result of market power). With one non-traded sector, we observe that the classic “Dutch disease” effect here would arise when one sector gets more productive and draws labor away from other sectors, creating scarcity and raising prices; but this is not what we expect from the introduction of labor-substituting AI. In contrast, our last model considers two non-traded sectors and CES/free entry, and the opportunity for discrete adoption of technology that replaces unskilled labor from the AI-using sector. When AI reduces unit costs and increases variety, it will not pull U from non-tradables, instead it will displace workers from the AI-using sector and lower wage due to diminishing returns in alternative sectors. Strategic upstream pricing of AI then harms welfare through unit-cost (usage fees) and variety (access fees) channels, with income leakage abroad. We derive an adoption frontier tying feasible usage prices to displaced workers’ outside options and show a monopolist typically prices on this boundary; capping one instrument shifts rents to the other. Broad gains for the adopting country relies on pressure (or regulation) on both usage and access fees and as well as policy that supports productive absorption of displaced labor. The framework clarifies when AI can lower real wages and aggregate welfare despite efficiency gains.

title: Probability Pricing
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics, New York University (NYU) - New York University and Imperial College London

detail.title: Probability Pricing
detail.abstract:
This paper develops probability pricing, extending cash flow pricing to quantify the willingness-to-pay for changes in probabilities. We show that the value of any marginal change in probabilities can be expressed as a standard asset-pricing formula with hypothetical cash flows derived from changes in the survival function. This equivalence between probability and cash flow valuation allows us to construct hedging strategies and systematically decompose individual and aggregate willingness-to-pay. Four applications examine the valuation of changes in the distribution of aggregate consumption, the efficiency effects of varying performance precision in principal-agent problems, and the welfare implications of public and private information.

title: Demand Elasticity in Dynamic Asset Pricing
affiliations: Stanford University, London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE), Central European University (CEU) and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Demand Elasticity in Dynamic Asset Pricing
detail.abstract:
Standard demand elasticity estimation treats investors' demand slopes as stable objects that can be traced out by exogenous residual supply shifts. We show this identification strategy fails in dynamic settings: supply shocks cause demand curves to tilt and shift through general equilibrium effects. The mechanism is intuitive—investors' demand depends on the entire distribution of current and future returns, including volatility, covariances, and correlations with investment opportunities. Supply shocks that change today's prices inevitably reshape future return distributions, moving the demand curve itself. We develop and calibrate a dynamic model to quantify this mismeasurement. The measured slope is approximately 40% of its conceptual counterpart, implying that demand curves are substantially steeper than estimated. This distortion operates through two channels: endogenous risk (altered volatility and covariances) and amplified intertemporal hedging (changed correlation with investment opportunities). The distortion remains sizable even for infinitesimal or purely transitory shocks.

title: Present Bias and Discount Rate Risk
affiliations: , BI Norwegian Business School and BI Norwegian Business School

detail.title: Present Bias and Discount Rate Risk
detail.abstract:
Recent evidence in the psychology literature suggests that individuals' degree of present bias varies with the state of nature and increases under stress. Consistent with this notion, we document, using survey data on individuals’ expected and realized consumption growth, that agents indeed tend to overconsume relative to their expectations and that the degree of such overconsumption is higher in bad times. We analyze the asset pricing implications of this bias and show that even if they control a small fraction of wealth, investors with time-varying degree of present bias cause substantial, priced discount rate risks that have first-order impact on the level and time-variation of asset risk premiums. The mechanism is distinct from that of models with time-varying preference parameters and that of models with biased expectations about aggregate outcomes.

We find evidence that immigration enforcement reduced test scores for both U.S.-born and foreign-born Spanish-speaking students while also reducing the likelihood that these students are involved in disciplinary incidents in schools. Both of these effects are more pronounced for students in middle and high schools.

title: Multivariate Ordered Discrete Response Models with Lattice Structures
affiliations: and University of London, Royal Holloway College - Department of Economics

detail.title: Multivariate Ordered Discrete Response Models with Lattice Structures
detail.abstract: We analyze multivariate ordered discrete response models with a lattice structure, modeling decision makers who narrowly bracket choices across multiple dimensions. These models map latent continuous processes into discrete responses using functionally independent decision thresholds. In a semiparametric framework, we model latent processes as sums of covariate indices and unobserved errors and derive conditions for identifying index parameters, thresholds, and the joint cumulative distribution function of the errors. For the parametric bivariate probit case, we separately derive identification of regression parameters and thresholds, and the correlation parameter, with the latter requiring additional covariate restrictions. We outline estimation approaches for semiparametric and parametric models, present simulations illustrating the performance of estimators for lattice models, and provide an application on the relationship between health and happiness rankings.

title: Then and Now: A Look Back and Ahead at the Federal Budget
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Department of Economics and Brookings Institution

detail.title: Then and Now: A Look Back and Ahead at the Federal Budget
detail.abstract:
It is well-understood that the U.S. faces an unsustainable fiscal future. We review historical budget trends and basic fiscal processes. We provide new estimates of the budget outlook, incorporating the recently enacted One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), and finding that the debt-GDP ratio will rise to 183% in 2054 under the OBBBA as legislated and to 199% if the temporary tax and spending provisions are made permanent. These figures compare to a current debt-GDP ratio of about 100% and a pre-OBBBA CBO analysis earlier this year that projected the 2054 debt-GDP ratio to be 154%. We estimate a fiscal gap – the permanent tax or spending changes needed to keep the 2054 debt-GDP ratio at its current level – to be about 3.4% of GDP if OBBBA is extended. We discuss the economic and political ramifications of debt and different ways to address the fiscal situation.

title: Does Regulation Distort Exit Decisions? Evidence from U.S. Power Plants
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Does Regulation Distort Exit Decisions? Evidence from U.S. Power Plants
detail.abstract:
Hundreds of power plants have closed in the United States since 2010, including 130+ gigawatts of coal and 50+ gigawatts of natural gas. In this paper, we highlight the potential for regulation to distort this type of exit decision. Using generator-level data from 2010–2023, we show that regulated units have been 45% less likely to exit than unregulated units. For unregulated units, exit decisions are made based on wholesale electricity prices, ongoing capital costs, and other traditional economic factors. In contrast, owners of regulated units are largely insulated from these factors and, in some cases, have a strong incentive to continue operating capital-intensive equipment. Previous work documents how this regulatory distortion affects investment decisions. Our paper emphasizes that these same incentives affect exit decisions as well.

title: The Consequences of Faculty Sexual Misconduct
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: The Consequences of Faculty Sexual Misconduct
detail.abstract:
Faculty sexual misconduct targeted at students is a widespread problem. The consequences of such incidents include direct harm to victims and may also entail a loss to science if students who encounter misconduct become discouraged from continuing their studies in their chosen field. We link publicly available information on degree completion by institution, academic field, and gender to a database of faculty sexual misconduct incidents verified in the media or court cases. Then, we employ a stacked event study approach to document the extent to which faculty sexual misconduct decreases in-field degree completion. Exposure to a field-specific faculty sexual misconduct incident decreases degree completion in that field by 3.4 percent four years after the incident. This decline is driven by incidents occurring after 2015, among which we observe a 7 percent decline in in-field degree completion. Students exit majors dominated by men, but this shift has little effect on predicted earnings because students shift away from both high- and low-earning majors.

title: How do Macroeconomic Conditions affect Banks’ Performance in Nigeria?

detail.title: How do Macroeconomic Conditions affect Banks’ Performance in Nigeria?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The Authors have no conflicting interest to declear

declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for the study

detail.abstract: This study examines how macroeconomic conditions influence Nigerian banks' performance, focusing on loan quality, profitability, and capital adequacy. Using quarterly data from 2010Q3 to 2025Q1, we apply a nonlinear autoregressive distributed lag (NARDL) framework to capture short-run and long-run asymmetries. The results show that macroeconomic shocks affect banks in asymmetric and time-dependent ways. GDP expansions reduce non-performing loans and support profitability but weaken capital adequacy by inflating risk-weighted assets, while contractions depress profitability and solvency. Inflation has mixed effects: moderate inflation boosts earnings through loan repricing, but sustained price pressures increase credit risk and erode capital buffers, while disinflation compresses margins. Exchange rate depreciation, modelled symmetrically, raises defaults and reduces solvency in the long run but has a transitory impact on profitability. The paper offers clear policy lessons: the need for countercyclical capital buffers to mitigate procyclical credit risks, the importance of inflation stabilisation as a foundation for financial soundness, and the necessity of active exchange rate risk management to reduce systemic exposure.

title: Branching Out: Capital Mobility and Long-Run Growth
affiliations: Vanderbilt University and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Branching Out: Capital Mobility and Long-Run Growth
detail.abstract:
We study the long-run effects of the first wave of U.S. banking market integration on capital mobility and manufacturing productivity. Using newly digitized bank and branch balance sheet data matched to state and county panels, we provide direct evidence that branching produced lasting productivity gains without aggregate capital deepening by leveraging internal capital markets to improve the geographic allocation of capital. Our novel ``deposit market access'' measure shows that bank funding grew most in capital-constrained counties within branching states. Both market access and border discontinuity designs indicate that branching’s organizational structure reduced capital allocation frictions to generate persistent growth.

title: Echoes of Waste: The Realities Behind RA 9003

detail.title: Echoes of Waste: The Realities Behind RA 9003
detail.abstract: This paper critically examines the implementation of Republic Act 9003, or the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, through an analysis of three studies conducted in Cabuyao City, Barangay Pansol of Quezon City, and a nationwide policy assessment by the Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS). The critique identifies both the strengths and limitations of these studies in addressing the local application of solid waste management policies. The findings highlight that while the law establishes a strong framework for sustainable waste management, challenges such as weak enforcement, inadequate facilities, limited funding, and low public awareness persist. The paper also discusses the importance of community engagement, institutional coordination, and behavioral change in enhancing policy effectiveness. Recommendations are proposed to strengthen local implementation through measurable performance indicators, public-private partnerships, and continuous education programs. Ultimately, this critique underscores that successful solid waste management requires more than compliance—it demands shared responsibility, sustained governance, and active citizen participation

title: The Economic Impact of Brexit
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, Bank of England, King’s College London - King's Business School, Deutsche Bundesbank and University of Nottingham

detail.title: The Economic Impact of Brexit
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the impact of the UK's decision to leave the European Union (Brexit) in 2016. Using almost a decade of data since the referendum, we combine simulations based on macro data with estimates derived from micro data collected through our Decision Maker Panel survey. These estimates suggest that by 2025, Brexit had reduced UK GDP by 6% to 8%, with the impact accumulating gradually over time. We estimate that investment was reduced by between 12% and 18%, employment by 3% to 4% and productivity by 3% to 4%. These large negative impacts reflect a combination of elevated uncertainty, reduced demand, diverted management time, and increased misallocation of resources from a protracted Brexit process. Comparing these with contemporary forecasts – providing a rare macro example to complement the burgeoning micro-literature of social science predictions – shows that these forecasts were accurate over a 5-year horizon, but they underestimated the impact over a decade.

detail.abstract:
This paper reexplores the assumption that female-headed households (FHH) often experience
lower standards of living compared to male-headed households (MHH) by addressing three of the gaps
found in the literature i) it uses a multidimensional poverty measure (MPI-LA); ii) employs objective
definitions for female headship based on economic and demographic characteristics; and iii) accounts for
household structure. Using cross-sectional data from the Nicaraguan Living Standards Measurement Study
(LSMS) 2014, the results indicate that FHH have lower levels of general poverty than MHH, regardless of
the headship definition used. However, differences in multidimensional poverty exist within FHH according
to the household structure. Co-resident MHH presents the highest multidimensional poverty levels, as
opposed to de facto FHH, which are found the least disadvantaged of all groups. Differences in severe
poverty are not as clear as those found in general poverty. A better measurement of household headship and
poverty can lead to better focalisation of poverty reduction programmes.

title: Restrictive Marriage Migration Policies and Family Outcomes
affiliations: University of Illinois at Chicago - Department of Economics and University of Illinois at Chicago

detail.title: Restrictive Marriage Migration Policies and Family Outcomes
detail.abstract:
As cross-border marriages rise, many governments have tightened rules on who can marry across borders, often in the name of promoting integration. Cross-border couples tend to have high divorce rates, which hinders successful assimilation. This paper provides the first evidence on how restrictive marriage migration policies affect family outcomes of migrants. We exploit a 2014 reform in South Korea that introduced pre-entry requirements for marriage visas, with language proficiency as the key component. Using rich administrative and survey data, we show that the reform led to a sharp temporary decline in cross-border marriages, improved migrants’ language skills, and increased educational attainment among both migrants and their Korean spouses. Comparing marriage cohorts immediately before and after the reform cutoff date, we find that cumulative divorce rates fell by 37% in the first 12 months and by 12% in the first 48 months, primarily due to language-based selection rather than demographic factors. Our evidence indicates that improved communication enhanced marital surplus and highlights the potential positive impact of selective admission policies that target civil and cultural assimilation.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether CEO organizational identification (OI) influences firms’ propensity to engage in myopic research and development (R&D) cuts. Using an archival-based measure of CEO OI, we find a negative association between CEO OI and the likelihood of reducing R&D expenditures to just meet analyst earnings forecasts. This result is consistent with the view that CEOs who strongly identify with their organizations are less willing to jeopardize innovation and long-term competitiveness for short-term performance. Cross-sectional analyses show that the negative relation is stronger in firms with greater innovation output but weaker when dedicated institutional ownership is higher. The findings remain robust when using alternative research designs to address endogeneity and to a placebo test that replaces R&D with capital investment. This study contributes to the literature by highlighting the role of CEO psychological orientation, measured using archival data, in shaping costly earnings management through myopic investment behavior.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the existence, magnitude and drivers of the sovereign greenium: the yield discount on sovereign and quasi-sovereign green bonds relative to conventional bonds. Using a dataset of 332 matched pairs of green and conventional bonds issued between 2014 and 2023 by sovereigns, sovereign-backed agencies, and multilateral development institutions, we analyze secondary-market pricing to capture both crosssectional and time-varying heterogeneity. We find a small but statistically significant greenium, averaging about 2 basis points for advanced economies and nearly 13 basis points for emerging markets. The greenium is larger for lower-rated issuers and increases when climate transition risks become more salient or when issuers are more vulnerable to climate change. Interaction effects indicate that global awareness of transition risks and domestic climate vulnerability jointly amplify the greenium. While green sovereign bonds trade at lower yields, the resulting fiscal savings are economically modest relative to total interest expenditures. A novel analysis of bond documentation shows that sovereign green bonds contain no binding commitments regarding environmental outcomes, suggesting that the observed greenium reflects symbolic rather than contractual sustainability value.
