publicationDetails.detailsText: Taxhells (2025). “Taxhells — 21st-Century Definition.” Taxhells Strategic Research White Paper, Geneva

detail.abstract: In traditional fiscal discourse, tax havens are jurisdictions offering low or no taxation, while “tax hells” describe those with high rates and bureaucratic excess. Yet this binary no longer reflects the fiscal reality of the 21st century. Modern taxation is defined not by monetary rates but by visibility — through continuous data extraction, compliance and behavioral control. This paper redefines “tax hells” as structural environments of fiscal overexposure, where the burden lies in informational surrender rather than payment. Drawing from Hansen & Kessler (2001), Martin Litwak, OECD transparency frameworks (CRS, FATCA, DAC7) and data-network governance research, it proposes a new analytical framework to understand the evolving architecture of global fiscal power.

title: Carbon leakage in heavy industry: evidence from satellite data
affiliations: Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), Organization for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD), Leverhulme Centre for Research on Globalisation and Economic Policy and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Carbon leakage in heavy industry: evidence from satellite data
detail.abstract: What is the effect of changes in carbon price on domestic emissions and international carbon leakage? This paper first develops a comprehensive plant-level carbon pricing dataset for key heavy industries at risk of carbon leakage, i.e. cement and steel, in 138 countries, drawing on satellite observations. The new dataset reveals that the average plant-level carbon price for these sectors increased by a factor of seven from USD 1.3 per tonne of CO2-equivalent (tCO2e) in January 2015 to USD 10.7/tCO2e in December 2021. Over the same time period, the average difference in carbon prices among trading partners, increased by more than 350%. The paper then tests whether higher carbon prices have reduced plant-level emissions and whether rising carbon price asymmetries across countries have affected international trade and led to carbon leakage. Results suggest that, on average, a USD 1/tCO2e increase in carbon prices reduces cement and steel plants’ emissions by 1.3%. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest that carbon leakage through international trade offset around 13% of these domestic emission reductions. ​

title: Convergent Validity in Incentive-Compatible Contingent Valuation: Bid-vector and elicitation format effects
affiliations: University of Warsaw, University of Warsaw, Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences (SLU), German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research (iDiv) Halle-Jena-Leipzig and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Convergent Validity in Incentive-Compatible Contingent Valuation: Bid-vector and elicitation format effects
detail.abstract: This study investigates convergent validity between elicitation formats within contingent valuation methodology, focusing on theory-driven formats designed to align with incentive compatibility. While earlier literature endorsed the single binary choice (SBC) format as the only incentive-compatible option, recent work outlines theoretical conditions under which payment card (PC) and open-ended (OE) formats may also encourage truthful preference revelation. Nevertheless, empirical findings have revealed limited convergent validity across formats, with behavioral biases proposed as an explanation. We contribute to this debate by directly comparing these three theory-driven (and arguably incentive-compatible) formats and assessing their robustness against bid-vector effects and other biases such as anchoring, yea-saying, and strategic misinterpretation. We conducted a large-scale, multi-country survey with 12,343 respondents across Poland, Sweden, Hungary, Spain, Germany, and the Netherlands, examining consumers’ willingness to pay (WTP) for an EU-wide biodiversity-enhancing program. Our analysis reveals significant discrepancies in WTP estimates across formats. However, analysis of choice frequencies suggests that convergent validity holds for lower bid levels, whereas higher bids introduce more pronounced divergences. We argue that these discrepancies stem from both behavioral biases and methodological factors, including bid vector design and econometric assumptions. Our results underscore the critical influence of bid structure on WTP estimates and highlight the need for further research to refine elicitation formats in contingent valuation studies. Finally, given pronounced differences in WTP estimates between SBC and PC formats, we suggest renewed consideration of the simple OE question as a viable elicitation format, as it avoids bid vector selection and thereby mitigates associated biases.

title: Can Tariffs Spur Higher Factory Floor Utilization?
affiliations: Federal Reserve Board of Governors, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Can Tariffs Spur Higher Factory Floor Utilization?

detail.abstract: Raising America's industrial output is a key goal of the recent increases in U.S. import tariffs. Domestic output could rise if positive effects of reduced foreign competition outweigh negative effects of increased policy uncertainty and complexity, higher costs of imported inputs, and retaliatory trade policy in export markets.

title: Between Resistance and Readiness Segment-Specific Reactions to Consumption Reduction
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of Duisburg-Essen

detail.title: Between Resistance and Readiness Segment-Specific Reactions to Consumption Reduction
detail.abstract: Limiting global warming to 1.5°C requires not only technological innovation but also substantial reductions in individual consumption, particularly in high-income societies. Yet sufficiency lifestyles are often perceived as sacrifices, creating motivational and psychological barriers. Effective communication is therefore essential but must move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches. Using a representative Austrian sample, we identify four consumer segments ranging from highly engaged to fully disengaged. These groups differ systematically in their expectations of sufficiency: the more engaged, the more positive the anticipated outcomes, and vice versa. Segment membership is also shaped by psychological needs, with autonomy and competence satisfaction predicting engagement, while autonomy frustration characterizes the disengaged. Based on these insights, we provide segment-specific recommendations for messages that minimize reactance and increase openness to behavior change. Our findings emphasize the motivational role of anticipated gains and losses and highlight the importance of audience-tailored framing for fostering sustainable consumption reduction.

title: The Distributional Impact of Environmental Policy Stringency in Europe
affiliations: University of Siegen and Justus-Liebig-Universität Gießen

detail.title: The Distributional Impact of Environmental Policy Stringency in Europe
detail.abstract: Environmental deterioration has become a pressing concern for policymakers, as reflected in initiatives such as the European Green Deal and Fit for 55, designed to steer the European Union and other OECD countries toward low-carbon development. This transition carries significant economic and social implications, with the potential for both desired and adverse impacts. To assess whether the positive or negative effects prevail, this study examines the distributional impacts of environmental policy stringency in European countries. It provides empirical evidence on the impact of policy adoption and stringency, measured by OECD’s Climate Actions and Policies Measurement Framework (CAPMF), on income inequality, using pre-tax, post-tax national income, and disposable income Gini coefficients. These three measures show the full redistributive effects of environmental policy in European countries. Employing a panel dataset covering 20 European countries over 32 years, the study addresses slope heterogeneity, cross-sectional dependence, and endogeneity using the Augmented Mean Group (AMG) estimator. The findings show that environmental policies initially increase inequality, disproportionately affecting lower-income groups. However, redistribution through taxation, in-kind transfers, and direct cash assistance neutralizes this effect, making disposable income inequality statistically insignificant. This underscores the role of social welfare mechanisms in ensuring an equitable green transition.  The results are robust to different econometric specifications. We conclude that in higher-income countries, increasingly rigorous environmental policies can have unintended adverse implications, but current redistributive policies can mitigate these effects.

title: Pennies Dropped; Dollars Raised: Using Information Architecture to Increase Retirement Savings
affiliations: , Voya Financial and Voya Financial

detail.title: Pennies Dropped; Dollars Raised: Using Information Architecture to Increase Retirement Savings

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The research was reviewed and approved by an independent IRB (Pearl IRB Protocol #2025-0255).

detail.abstract: Across two studies conducted with U.S. participants, we establish that the way in which retirement contributions are presented can influence savings intentions, perceptions, and behavior. We propose a dollars-based frame that presents retirement savings as dollar amounts contributed for every $100 of income (e.g., “dollars per $100 earned”). A lab experiment with 500 individuals comparing five retirement contribution frames (Pennies; Dollars; Percent; Fractional Percent; Fractional Dollars and Cents) found that dollars-based framing was easiest for participants to understand and was most associated with the perception of saving affordability. A subsequent field experiment examining the real-world savings behavior of 10,849 retirement plan participants found that framing retirement savings as “dollars per $100 earned” (dollars-based framing) led to greater savings compared to “percent of what I earn” (percent-based framing) and to “pennies per dollar earned” (pennies-based framing). This dollars-based framing approach helped participants save more, particularly lower-income savers. As pennies lose their economic, cultural, and behavioral salience, dollars-based framing emerges as a more effective strategy to boost retirement savings. These findings contribute to a broader understanding of how the effectiveness of behavioral interventions can shift over time and across contexts.

title: Awareness, Usage, and Service Delivery of the eGov PH Mobile Application: Socio-Demographic Variations and Insights from the Good Governance Model

detail.title: Awareness, Usage, and Service Delivery of the eGov PH Mobile Application: Socio-Demographic Variations and Insights from the Good Governance Model

detail.abstract: This study explores the implementation and citizen evaluation of the eGov PH mobile app, a government platform that aggregates essential public services in the Philippines. Guided by four objectives, the research outlines the socio-demographic profiles of users, assesses awareness, effectiveness, challenges, and recommendations, explores significant differences in evaluations across groups, and offers policy suggestions. Using a systematic literature review (SLR) guided by PRISMA 2020, recent academic studies, government reports, and policy briefs from 2017 to 2024 were synthesized. Findings revealed that younger, urban, professional, and highly educated citizens are more active users, while older, rural, selfemployed, and less-educated groups face greater barriers. In terms of awareness and usage, familiarity strongly influenced adoption, with accessibility and ease of use driving engagement. Effectiveness was noted in reducing in-person transactions and streamlining service delivery, although disparities in digital literacy and infrastructure limited inclusivity. Key challenges identified included limited connectivity, uneven ICT readiness, low digital literacy, and cybersecurity concerns. Suggestions emphasized usercentered design, training programs, stronger data protection, and expanded broadband access. Comparative assessments revealed significant differences across socio-demographic profiles, underscoring the existence of digital inequality.In conclusion, the review emphasizes that although the eGov PH mobile app shows promise for efficient and transparent governance, inclusive strategies that address demographic and infrastructural disparities are crucial. It is recommended that policymakers and developers prioritize digital literacy, security, and equitable access to ICT to fully realize citizen-centered e-governance.

title: Retail Traders with Strict Stop-Loss can Win Big
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Retail Traders with Strict Stop-Loss can Win Big
detail.abstract: Most retail traders fail to achieve consistent profitability in financial markets. The reasons often include emotional decision-making, lack of planning, and the absence of discipline. Trading with real money introduces fear and greed, making rational execution difficult. However, one element that can tilt the odds in favor of retail traders is disciplinespecifically, maintaining a predefined target and stop-loss. This paper presents a simple probabilistic analogy: if a trader gains 3 units when correct and loses 1 unit when wrong, like repeatedly tossing a coin where heads yield +3 and tails-1, the long-term expected outcome becomes positive even with a 50%-win rate. By focusing on asymmetric risk-reward setups and consistent execution, retail traders can build sustainable profitability over time. This framework emphasizes the mathematical power of discipline and repetition in trading success.

title: The Constitution of Innovation: A New European Renaissance
affiliations: European University Institute - Department of Law (LAW), Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and European University Institute

detail.title: The Constitution of Innovation: A New European Renaissance
detail.abstract: Every other year, a new report sounds the alarm of Europe's secular economic decline. The message is unambiguous: Europe is getting poorer; the US and China are getting richer. For the old continent, the issue is existential. Without growth, the welfare state, free pensions, lifelong education, and universal healthcare will be a utopia of the past. These reports are symptoms of a deeper issue: the European Union (EU) has abandoned its core mandate of economic integration. Instead, EU institutions have embraced a defensive, regulation-first approach, believing that rulemaking is Europe’s ‘superpower’ and that the “Brussels Effect” will set global rules. This theory is failing in practice. The US has not adopted EU rules, and China co-opts them to serve its own government objectives. The upshot is not global influence, but excessive bureaucratization that stifles home-grown innovation. To reverse course, the EU must undergo a radical reorientation of its priorities: it must adopt a single-minded focus on prosperity, do less but better, embrace economic dynamism and creative destruction, and enforce genuine mutual recognition. That vision can be operationalized through six practical reforms designed to reinvigorate competitiveness.

title: Market Power Increase and Sectoral Heterogeneity: The Role of e-Commerce Platforms

detail.title: Market Power Increase and Sectoral Heterogeneity: The Role of e-Commerce Platforms
detail.abstract: This paper studies the impact of e-commerce platforms on firms' market power. I present a model with firm heterogeneity, oligopolistic competition, and Input-Output linkages, in which firms use the platforms to lower their variable costs. The cost reduction can occur either (i) as a result of efficiency gains or (ii) via direct discounts on input prices. The increasing use of platforms contributes to the rise of market power because it transforms the cost structure of the firms. Platform users show lower marginal costs but higher overhead costs: since the benefits of the marginal costs reduction outweigh the increase in overhead costs, this gives them a competitive advantage, explaining the increase in market power. Once calibrated to US data, the model attributes one third of the increase in markups to the introduction of e-commerce platforms. At the sectoral level, the heterogeneity in platforms use explains up to 40% of the differences in market power trends across sectors.

title: Application of Intelligent Incremental Model for Predicting ExhaustGas Temperature of Aircraft Engines
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Northwestern Polytechnic University (NPU)

detail.title: Application of Intelligent Incremental Model for Predicting ExhaustGas Temperature of Aircraft Engines
detail.abstract: The prediction of exhaust gas temperature (EGT) is crucial for aircraft engine health management (EHM) and flight safety. Most studies focus on developing EGT prediction models using neural networks because of their capacity to extract nonlinear features from engine data. However, the performance of these models is often hindered by the oversight of data distribution differences from various flight missions. In this paper, we propose a novel intelligent-incremental model to enhance EGT prediction accuracy during long-term flight. Specifically, physical architecture-driven structure is designed for extracting physical feature from each flight. Three transfer paradigms (flight boundary, feature, and model parameter) are introduced to transfer historical information and address flight domain discrepancies. Then, these paradigms are integrated to form the incremental learning framework for the EGT model in the absence of historical flight data. Extensive experiments on long-term flight datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of these paradigms, showing improved model accuracy for different neural network types. The incremental EGT model demonstrates superior predictive performance, reducing errors by 22.86% and 36.61% on two datasets compared to non-incremental results. Furthermore, performance degradation tests show a favorable decreasing trend, confirming the proposed method's engineering applicability, particularly in long-term operations and maintenance of aircraft engine.

title: Superstars or Super-Villains? Productivity Spillovers and Firm Dynamics in Indonesia

detail.title: Superstars or Super-Villains? Productivity Spillovers and Firm Dynamics in Indonesia

detail.abstract: Do industrial "superstars" help others up or crowd them out? We examine the relationship between the spillovers of superstar firms (those with the top market share in their industry) and the productivity dynamics in Indonesia. Employing data on Indonesian manufacturing firms from 2001 to 2015, we find that superstar exposures in the market raise both the productivity level and the growth of non-superstar firms through horizontal (within a sector-province) and vertical (across sectors) channels. When we distinguish by ownership, foreign superstars consistently encourage productivity except through the horizontal channel. In contrast, domestic superstars generate positive spillovers through both horizontal and vertical linkages, indicating that foreign firms do not solely drive positive externalities. Furthermore, despite overall productivity growth being positive in 2001-2015, the source of negative growth is mainly driven by within-group reallocation-evidence of misallocation among surviving firms-notably by domestic superstars. Although Indonesian superstar firms are more efficient in their operations, their relatively modest growth rates suggest a potential stagnation, which can be plausibly attributed to limited innovation activity or a slow pace of adopting new technologies.

title: Winners and Losers: How Corporate Tax Reforms Reshape the Firm Distribution
affiliations: and Erasmus University Rotterdam

detail.title: Winners and Losers: How Corporate Tax Reforms Reshape the Firm Distribution
detail.abstract: We study how corporate tax reforms affect the distribution of resources across firms. Motivated by a Dutch fiscal reform, we use a heterogeneous firm model to test whether a lower tax rate coupled with reduced investment deductibility improves allocative efficiency. We find that aggregate productivity increases and capital misallocation declines, driven by the reallocation of capital from mediumlarge firms to the largest and most productive. The tax cut disproportionately benefits top firms, enabling their expansion, while the deductibility reduction burdens medium-large firms that invest more intensively than others.

title: Is Donald Trump Winning the Trade War?
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Is Donald Trump Winning the Trade War?
detail.abstract:
By any measure, the trade policy of the second Donald Trump administration surprised many. April 2, 2025, so-called Liberation Day, would not be forgotten easily. On that day, President Trump signed two executive orders and announced a long list of unilateral across-the-board tariffs involving all countries. In the terminology of the executive order, the “reciprocal” tariffs were primarily intended to “rectify trade practices that contribute to large and persistent annual United States goods trade deficits.” No country escaped higher tariffs; even those that ran bilateral deficits with the United States were subject to a 10% levy. What to make of these drastic policy announcements that introduced a period of unprecedented policy uncertainty in the United States? This case brings in a new geoeconomic perspective, and explicitly ties in the work of Albert Hirschman, arguably the founder of this field that links international economics and international relations (power). At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, this case is taught in the “Managing International Trade and Investment” MBA elective. It can also be taught on its own or as part of a mini-module on trade policy along with related cases and technical notes. It is critical, however, that this case be taught together with the following technical note: Peter Debaere, “National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade and the New Geoeconomics,” UVA-GEM-0253. The note provides a framework, grounded in geoeconomics and Hirschman's pioneering work, that will give students a new way to think about US trade policy.

Excerpt

Is Donald Trump Winning the Trade War?

By any measure, the trade policy of the second Donald Trump administration surprised many. April 2, 2025, so-called Liberation Day, would not be forgotten easily. On that day, President Trump pursued, according to the White House Fact Sheet, “reciprocity to rebuild the economy and restore national and economic security,” following “the golden rule for our golden age: Today's action simply asks other countries to treat us like we treat them…Access to the American market is a privilege, not a right.” In the White House Rose Garden, the president signed two executive orders. He announced a long list of unilateral, across-the-board tariffs involving all countries, with levels at, for example, 34% for China, 20% for the European Union (EU), 46% for Vietnam, 32% for Taiwan, 24% for Japan, and 26% for India. In the terminology of the executive order, the “reciprocal” tariffs were primarily intended to “rectify trade practices that contribute to large and persistent annual United States goods trade deficits.” The US overall trade deficit with the rest of the world was 3.1% of GDP in 2024, up from 2.8% in 2023. No country escaped higher tariffs; even those that ran bilateral deficits with the United States were subject to a 10% levy.

The reciprocal tariffs announced on April 2 were not the first trade actions by the administration. They had been preceded by an initial salvo of 25% on all imports of cars, car parts, and steel and aluminum, including for Canada and Mexico, countries with which Trump had negotiated the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement (USMCA) in his first term. An escalating tariff war with China also had already run out of hand. Bilateral tariffs ratcheted up above 100%, levels at which virtually no trade was viable. Eventually, a ceasefire was agreed upon, returning both countries’ tariffs to much lower levels (at least temporarily). Other nations also received a temporary break from the reciprocal tariffs. They faced a uniform tariff of 10% for most goods, in addition to the earlier 25% sectoral tariffs. The pause was intended to bring the countries to the negotiation table with the administration, or, in the words of the president, “to kiss my ass."

Since then, the United States had made “deals” with individual countries. Keir Starmer, prime minister of the United Kingdom, was very eager to reach a first deal. More deals with Japan, the EU, South Korea, and others followed. Some countries were simply sent a letter from the administration with their specific new rate. By the end of the summer of 2025, additional new rates were made public. In August 2025, most UK goods, for example, got a 10% levy, and the EU, Japan, and South Korea had to live with 15%. Laos, on the other hand, was to face 40%, and Switzerland was shocked to learn after a phone call between its president and Trump that it could expect a levy of 39%. Brazil was threatened with 50%. To be clear, all these bilateral “deals” were more like framework agreements: Unlike usual trade agreements, which typically took years to negotiate and were much more detailed, these left many issues unresolved or unclear. . . .

title: An Introduction to Private Equity Secondaries
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and

detail.title: An Introduction to Private Equity Secondaries
detail.abstract:
This technical note introduce readers to two types of secondary market transactions in the private equity space: limited-partner-led (LP-led) secondaries and general-partner-led (GP-led) secondaries. It explains the process of creating a continuation vehicle, outlines the key stakeholders involved, and highlights potential conflicts of interest among them. Finally, it describes the dynamic of the secondary market and the largest players in the space.

Excerpt

An Introduction to Private Equity Secondaries

Governed by limited partnership agreements (LPAs), private equity (PE) funds are intended to be self-liquidating at the end of their lives. These funds call for the limited partners (LPs) to commit capital for at least 10 years. Yet LPs frequently face liquidity shocks that create pressure to cash out from existing illiquid PE commitments before the end of a fund's life. The presence of such liquidity shocks made the development of the PE secondary market (secondaries) both necessary and inevitable. Contrary to primary investments, where funds were invested or committed directly to a fund or a company, secondaries involved either selling LPs' existing fund commitments to new LPs (LP-led secondaries) or moving portfolio companies to a new fund (general partner–led [GP-led] secondaries).

The very first secondaries trade is believed to have been made in the late 1970s by venture capitalist (VC) Dayton Carr. International Business Machines Corporation (IBM) CEO Thomas Watson was selected by President Jimmy Carter to become ambassador to the USSR in 1979, and Watson was required to dispose of his personal holdings in a few private VC funds before taking office. Carr raised the money to buy Watson's positions from him.

Forty-five years later, PE secondaries have become an integral part of the private capital industry, LPs' portfolio construction, and GPs' liquidity options (Exhibit 1). In 2025, secondary transactions reached their highest volume in history, estimated at around $100 billion in expected deal value and growing at 40% annually since 2020. By mid-2025, secondaries funds accumulated $171 billion of “dry powder” and included some of the largest private funds in the world chasing a run-rate investment opportunity set of about $190 billion.

LP-Led Secondaries

LP-led secondaries (Exhibit 2) emerged as a response to LPs' need to manage liquidity shocks. In these transactions, LPs sell their interests in PE funds to other investors before the funds reach maturity. Buyers effectively assume both the seller's outstanding unfunded commitments and the seller's share of invested capital in the underlying portfolio companies. While GPs do not directly control these transactions, their consent is often required, and their involvement can meaningfully shape deal structure and execution.

title: Intertwined Network Effects: Theory and Evidence
affiliations: Joint Research Centre (European Commission)

detail.title: Intertwined Network Effects: Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract: In many transaction two-sided markets, an "aggregator" platform (e.g., Trivago) gives buyers access to the sellers (e.g., hotels) of a competing "source" platform (e.g., Booking). This creates "intertwined network effects" (INE) between them. Despite the prevalence of this phenomenon, including multiple prominent mergers, its welfare implications remain understudied. Using a theoretical model, I show that while INE increase consumer surplus, they reduce seller surplus if the platforms are sufficiently differentiated for sellers, and increase it otherwise. In presence of INE, a non-consolidating merger reduces double marginalization, but increases market power. Thus, it harms consumers if the network effects they enjoy are sufficiently low, and vice versa. If the platforms are sufficiently homogeneous to sellers, the merger reduces their surplus. I empirically validate the model's predictions on consumer and seller participation by exploiting two cases in which classified ads platforms introduced INE: Finn/Nettbil and Adverts/DoneDeal. Using event study designs, I show that INE caused an increase in the number of users in the aggregator. Using a time series approach, I provide descriptive evidence that INE increased seller participation in the aggregator and decreased it in the source platform. I discuss the implications of the findings for merger control and asymmetric interoperability policies.

title: Is Big Lots in Big Trouble?
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: Is Big Lots in Big Trouble?
detail.abstract:
By the middle of 2023, previous market darling and star performer Big Lots suddenly found itself facing possible bankruptcy. CEO Bruce Thorn needed a vision for Big Lots that would establish near-term financial viability and also inspire confidence in the business’s long-term prospects. While the sudden decline could be attributed to short-term factors, notably inflation-driven fears curtailing demand and temporary supply chain disruptions, the viability of the Big Lots business model was also in doubt. The case provides information sufficient to build a two-year forecast and to benchmark that forecast performance against peers. Classroom discussions will focus on the technical aspects of forecasting, the selection and meaning of leverage metrics, and how business decisions manifest in financial statements. At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, this case is used in the first-year finance curriculum in a module focused on optimal capital structure. It would also be suitable in courses that introduce or explore financial forecasting.

Excerpt

Is Big Lots in Big Trouble?

At the start of 2022, Bruce Thorn, the CEO of Big Lots, Inc. (Big Lots), had good reason to be optimistic about the company’s prospects. With plans to add 50 new stores that year and increase the pace of expansion to 80 stores a year, the company was emerging from a period of market uncertainty with a clear vision for success, a vision embodied in its Operation North Star strategy unveiled in 2019. That strategy envisioned revenue rising from about $6 billion to somewhere between $8 billion and $10 billion, along with enhanced margins. As Thorn noted at the time, “We see a clear and long runway for growth ahead of us, coupled with the opportunity to drive returns through margin expansion and judicious capital allocation.”

By the middle of 2023, however, Thorn was striking a very different tone. “For the past year and a half, we’ve been playing defense as the consumer environment quickly and sharply deteriorated. High inflation has disproportionately impacted our lower-income customers, who have delayed or pulled back spending on discretionary items, particularly in high ticket home and seasonal categories,” he said. In addition, supply chain disruptions at the time had proved especially challenging for Big Lots, including the closure of its key furniture supplier. The impact on financial performance had been striking. Total revenue in 2022 declined by more than 10%, largely driven by a decline of 25% in the furniture category (Exhibit 1 shows sales by category). Margins as a percentage of revenue also declined, and Big Lots suffered a net loss for the year (Exhibits 2 and 3 present income statements and balance sheets, respectively). The situation deteriorated further during the first half of 2023 (see Exhibit 4 for midyear results). By October of 2023, CreditRiskMonitor estimated Big Lots had a 4% to 10% chance of being bankrupt within 12 months.

A major concern for businesses facing financial challenges was that their difficulties could become self-reinforcing. Precisely when a firm needed to make changes to improve performance, stakeholders could respond in ways that made those changes more difficult. Observing the company at the time, Credit Suisse analysts led by Karen Short noted that “we expect concerns around the potential for vendors to significantly tighten credit terms or (in the worst case) stop supply to persist.” Such changes would weaken the firm when it needed to be strong. Survival required Big Lots, as Thorn put it, to be “very aggressive in how we are managing our business.” Some of those actions, like the company’s announced plans to cut $100 million in selling, general, and administrative expenses, would unsettle its workforce. Other actions, like promotions to bring inventory down to levels appropriate for lower sales volume, would harm margins in the short run. Even cautious moves that improved the company’s financial position, like the recently announced suspension of dividends, rattled investors.

title: GoFundMe, Inc.: AI Opportunities?
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business and University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: GoFundMe, Inc.: AI Opportunities?
detail.abstract:
When Arnie Katz (Darden MBA '09) joined privately held GoFundMe, Inc. (GoFundMe), as chief product and technology officer in August 2023, he asked one simple question: “How are we using artificial intelligence?” The question came nine months after OpenAI had released an early version of ChatGPT. Katz and Karan Khurana, product leader at GoFundMe, examined the process steps to start and activate a fundraising campaign (what they called the “create funnel”) and in doing so pulled together data on time spent at each process step and on drop-off rates, meaning the number of people who logged in to start a fundraising campaign but ultimately stopped at some point in the process. What opportunities did AI offer GoFundMe? This field-based case offers a history of GoFundMe and an overview of its processes. At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, it is taught in the second-year elective “Digital Operations Strategy” and in the core operations course in the first year. It would also be suitable in any course seeking to examine how generative AI can change core business processes and push students to rethink and not just automate.

Excerpt

GoFundMe, Inc.: AI Opportunities?

When Arnie Katz (Darden MBA '09) joined privately held GoFundMe, Inc. (GoFundMe), as chief product and technology officer in August 2023, he asked one simple question: “How are we using artificial intelligence [AI]?” The question came nine months after OpenAI had released an early version of ChatGPT. “The chatbot quickly went viral on social media as users shared examples of what it could do,” wrote a Forbes contributor. “Stories and samples included everything from travel planning to writing fables to code computer programs. Within five days, the chatbot had attracted over one million users.” Katz found that GoFundMe had been slow to react: “The R&D team was busy working on the planned roadmap and lacking the context of how revolutionary the technology was coupled with some fears around using it. The entire Silicon Valley is upending full product roadmaps to react to the new GenAI world.” Katz was meeting with Karan Khurana, product leader at GoFundMe, to discuss use cases for AI at the crowdfunding platform. The two had previously worked together at Uber and Walmart eCommerce and were comfortable challenging each other's ideas and assumptions.

The Giving Layer of the Internet

In 2010, cofounders Brad Damphousse and Andrew Ballester had started GoFundMe (and launched GoFundMe.com) to help charities raise money online, but they soon found that the majority of its users were individuals trying to raise money for personal causes and life events. “It's people experiencing the long-tail of everyday life,” said Damphousse, referring to “everything from weddings to funerals, education, youth sports, animals and pets. It's a place where family, friends, and communities, come together to support one another.”

title: National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade and the New Geoeconomics
affiliations: University of Virginia - Darden School of Business

detail.title: National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade and the New Geoeconomics
detail.abstract:
Geoeconomists combine economics and political science to study how governments use their countries' economic strength to exert influence (power) on foreign entities over which they tend not to have direct control, to induce those entities to take actions that they would not otherwise take. In the rapidly shifting geopolitical environment of the first quarter of the 21st century, geoeconomics offers a new way to think about US trade policy. The theory and empirics in Albert Hirschman's 1945 classic, National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade, were foundational for the discipline. This note offers an overview of Hirschman's views on trade as an instrument of national power, then touches on some more recent developments in the field.At the University of Virginia Darden School of Business, this note is taught in the “Managing International Trade and Investment” MBA elective, together with a related case: Peter Debaere, “Is Donald Trump Winning the Trade War?” (UVA-GEM-0252).

National Power and the Structure of Foreign Tradeand the New Geoeconomics

Geoeconomics is a field that combines economics and political science. Geoeconomists study how governments use their countries' economic strength to exert influence on foreign entities over which they tend not to have direct control, to induce those entities to take actions that they would not otherwise take. To be fair, economists have until recently paid little attention to geoeconomics. In the rapidly shifting geopolitical environment of the first quarter of the 21st century, however, that is changing. Albert Hirschman's 1945 classic, National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade, is making something of a comeback, for it was this book's theory and empirics that, one could argue, were foundational for the discipline.

Hirschman: Weaponizing International Trade

For Hirschman, an international economist, the link between economics and politics was real and personal. A Jew born in Berlin, he fled Weimar Germany in 1933, fought fascism in Italy, and, before coming to the United States in 1940 himself, assisted other Jews desperate to leave Europe. His pioneering book National Power and the Structure of Foreign Trade focuses on the politicization of international trade and brings international economics and international affairs together. Hirschman studied how, and under what conditions, a sovereign country can use trade as an instrument of national power and exploit weaknesses in the system of trade most effectively.

detail.abstract: We develop a novel, scalable method for assessing the quality of public procurement systems using standard administrative data. We first derive a simple theoretical benchmark that relates the expected distribution of contract value winning firms, measured as a Herfindahl-Hirschman index (HHI), to the distribution of auction values, measured as a respective HHI, and the number of winning firms. It argues that the 21st century’s crises, war, inequality, climate degradation, and corruption, are not merely political or economic failures but symptoms of a deeper leadership fracture. This paper, Kenya’s ESG Disclosure Maturity and Africa’s Path from Reporting to Risk Pricing, examines how Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) disclosure is transforming from a reporting exercise into a determinant of capital allocation across African markets. Using data from the Risk Insights ESG GPS™ platform for 2023/2024, the study benchmarks Kenya’s ESG maturity against South Africa’s, revealing distinct trajectories in environmental, social, and governance transparency. For Kenya, 32% of listed firms disclose Net Zero commitments, while only 12.5% report Scope 1 and 2 emissions, and 7% report Scope 3 emissions. Water and waste disclosure remain minimal, at 18% and 3.6%, respectively. South Africa demonstrates broader coverage (30–36% across environmental metrics) but limited depth in performance-based reporting. Despite progress in board diversity and governance transparency, both markets face significant challenges in assurance, standardized frameworks, and procurement disclosure.

The paper argues that ESG data has become a proxy for market credibility, directly influencing access to capital, credit spreads, and sovereign risk pricing. By aligning with IFRS S1/S2, GRI, TCFD, and CSRD, African issuers can integrate into global sustainable finance ecosystems and qualify for green, social, and sustainability-linked (GSS+) instruments in a bond market exceeding USD 5 trillion. Empirical insights show that firms with robust ESG disclosure in emerging markets achieve up to 20 basis points lower borrowing costs, underscoring the financial value of transparency.

The study concludes that Africa’s transition from reporting to risk pricing hinges on three pillars: (1) regulatory enforcement of standardized ESG templates, (2) assurance and data comparability across exchanges, and (3) integration of Africa-native ESG intelligence into investment models. Moving from symbolic disclosure to measurable impact will position African markets as credible participants in the next generation of sustainable capital flows.

detail.abstract: The Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) sector holds strategic importance for Azerbaijan's ambitions to diversify beyond hydrocarbons and modernize its national economy. Yet, despite extensive public investment and infrastructure development, the sector's contribution to GDP, employment, and exports remains limited. Drawing on official statistics and policy documents for 2020-2025, this study examines the performance, structure, and constraints of Azerbaijan's ICT and digital economy. In 2024, ICT accounted for only 1.8 percent of GDP, 0.036 percent of total exports, and 1.4 percent of national employment. Research and development (R&D) expenditure remained below 0.3 percent of GDP, while Azerbaijan ranked 94th in the 2025 Global Innovation Index-well behind regional peers. The paper attributes the sector's underperformance to low innovation intensity, weak private-sector participation, and overreliance on state-led infrastructure projects such as Azercosmos, which, while symbolically important, have not produced broad technological spillovers. At the same time, Azerbaijan has made measurable progress in digital finance, with non-cash payments rising from 30 percent in 2021 to 64.2 percent in 2024. These advances, however, have not translated into a robust, innovation-driven ICT ecosystem. The findings suggest that Azerbaijan's digital transformation remains infrastructure-heavy but innovation-light, requiring a shift toward policies that promote R&D investment, entrepreneurial capacity, and integration into global digital value chains.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the design of sparse networks that support large matchings under adversarial vertex deletions (vertex interdiction). Unlike prior literature that assumes i.i.d. disruptions, we consider the adversarial setting and explore the structural properties of optimal networks. We first study the sparsest graph that supports the same matching size as the complete graph and find that connected structures - particularly, the chain-type graphs - are optimal under certain conditions. However, when sparsity constraints become more stringent relative to the number of deleted vertices, disconnected structures - such as cluster-type graphs (disjoint unions of cliques) - can be optimal. We analyze the performance of regular chains and clusters, illustrating the transition from chains to clusters as the better design. Our analysis suggests that the latter is more robust to disruption (both in terms of the mode of disruption and the number of vertices deleted), making it more advantageous in high-stress environments.

detail.abstract: Young adults today face unprecedented mental health challenges, yet many hesitate to seek support due to barriers such as accessibility, stigma, and time constraints. detail.abstract:
India’s education system continues to face persistent challenges in access and quality. We
examine the role and constraints of private sector participation by combining historical, legal, and
judicial analysis with primary research in the form of stakeholder interviews. We review India’s
ideological and constitutional precedents to trace how national ideals have shaped an unfriendly policy climate for private providers. We then analyze key regulations and court judgements, supplemented with interviews of parents, school administrators, and ed-tech founders to assess ground-level realities. We find that while private schools serve nearly half of students in India and are perceived by parents as superior to government schools across infrastructure, accountability, and outcomes, though they remain restricted by fee caps, nonprofit mandates, and administrative compliance burdens. Our results suggest that regulatory and ideological barriers constrain private initiatives to innovate, invest, and develop and run private institutions. We argue for reforms emphasizing streamlined approvals, outcome-based policy, and public-private partnerships to unlock the private sector’s potential while balancing equity in access.

detail.abstract: The Entropic Markov Wealth Model (EMWM) presents a novel method for forecasting financial sustainability by integrating entropy-based disorder measures and behavioral-energy coefficients into a probabilistic state model. The framework models transitions among key wealth states-Growth, Drift, Decay, and Renewal-through entropy-weighted probabilities that reflect dynamic behavioral patterns and external influences. It introduces a Wealth Stability Index (WSI), quantifying systemic resilience and behavioral bias effects in individual, corporate, and national financial systems. This paper provides a conceptual overview of the model, mathematical logic, and use cases across financial forecasting, portfolio optimization, and macroeconomic stability assessment.

detail.abstract: The synergy of the KLC approach components (knowledge, learning, and collaboration cultures) supports a knowledge-driven organization's sustainability. detail.title: One Size Doesn't Fit All: Exploring Gendered Insights into Job Satisfaction and Employee Retention in HEI in India
detail.abstract: This study investigates the determinants of job satisfaction and their impact on employee retention within Higher Education Institutions (HEIs), with job satisfaction serving as a mediating variable and gender as a moderating factor. Employing a robust hybrid Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) approach, the study analyzes the influence of five key antecedents-compensation, work environment, job security, career advancement, and recognition-on job satisfaction and, in turn, on retention. The results reveal that all five factors significantly and positively contribute to job satisfaction, with job security and career advancement emerging as the most influential. Job satisfaction was found to significantly enhance employee retention, underscoring its pivotal role in sustaining a committed academic workforce. The multi-group analysis (MGA) identified gender-based differences, with male employees prioritizing compensation and job security, while female employees showed a stronger preference for a supportive work environment. However, both genders equally valued career advancement and recognition. These findings offer valuable insights for HEI administrators and policymakers, suggesting the need for holistic, inclusive, and demographically sensitive HR strategies that foster long-term commitment and institutional effectiveness.

title: Ethical and Managerial Challenges in Elder Care Institutions
affiliations: Oxford Academy and George Mason University

detail.title: Ethical and Managerial Challenges in Elder Care Institutions
detail.abstract: Elder-care institutions play a vital role in supporting ageing populations, yet they operate in environments marked by complex ethical, managerial, and societal challenges. As longevity increases worldwide, care systems face pressure to balance quality, autonomy, and accountability while responding to limited resources and workforce constraints. This doctoral thesis investigates the ethical and managerial dilemmas confronting elder-care institutions, focusing on how leadership, organisational culture, and professional ethics interact to shape the quality of care and the dignity of older adults. Using a qualitative narrative-synthesis methodology, this research integrates evidence from international literature, policy frameworks, and case studies spanning Europe, North America, and Asia (2015-2025). The study applies an ethical-decision-making and adaptive-leadership framework to explore tensions between institutional efficiency and human-centred care. It identifies recurrent ethical challenges, including staff shortages, moral distress, neglect risks, and the balancing of residents' autonomy with safety and legal compliance. Findings reveal that effective elder-care management depends not solely on regulations or technical competence but on ethical leadership, organisational empathy, and a culture of moral accountability. Institutions with participatory management, transparent communication, and structured ethics training demonstrate higher staff satisfaction and reduced ethical conflict. The thesis proposes an Ethical-Managerial Integration Framework (EMIF) to guide decision-making, aligning ethical principles with managerial pragmatism and care quality. The study contributes to the fields of gerontology, healthcare management, and applied ethics by offering a multi-level understanding of elder-care governance. It calls for rehumanising institutional care through compassion-led leadership, continuous professional development, and ethically informed policy design that respects both carers and care recipients.

title: An Analysis of U.S. Public Pension Fund Allocations to Cryptocurrency and Precious Metals

detail.title: An Analysis of U.S. Public Pension Fund Allocations to Cryptocurrency and Precious Metals
detail.abstract: The investment strategies of U.S. public pension funds are critical to fiscal stability. Confronted with return challenges and elevated liabilities, these funds are diversifying into alternative assets with differentiated risk-return profiles. This study examines a measurable trend: allocations to cryptocurrency-related equities and precious metals. Using quarterly Form 13F-HR filings (Q1 2024-Q2 2025) for seventeen major funds, we quantify the scale and structure of these exposures, which grew to $3.3 billion (crypto) and $2.2 billion (metals) by mid-2025. Our central finding is a strong and growing institutional preference for indirect exposure through equity proxies like MicroStrategy and Newmont Corporation, rather than direct ownership or ETF positions. This indicates a cautious approach to incorporating new asset classes, balancing innovation within traditional fiduciary and governance frameworks. The results illuminate the evolving role of alternative assets in long-term public investment strategy.

title: Developing Life Skills Training Models for Mental Health Professionals
affiliations: Oxford Academy and George Mason University

detail.title: Developing Life Skills Training Models for Mental Health Professionals
detail.abstract:
The increasing prevalence of mental-health challenges worldwide demands not only clinical competence among mental-health professionals but also holistic life skills — including communication, empathy, emotional intelligence, ethical reasoning, and resilience. These human competencies are essential for maintaining well-being, professionalism, and ethical integrity within emotionally demanding work environments.

This doctoral study investigates how life skills training can be systematically integrated into mental-health education and professional development frameworks. Using a qualitative narrative-synthesis methodology, the research analyses theoretical and empirical literature published between 2015 and 2025, alongside global training models and policy frameworks. The objective is to construct a Life Skills Competency Development Framework (LSCDF) tailored to the needs of mental-health professionals, bridging the gap between clinical knowledge and personal mastery.

Findings reveal that life skills such as emotional regulation, reflective communication, leadership, and ethical self-awareness significantly enhance therapeutic effectiveness, teamwork, and client satisfaction. However, the study identifies major barriers including limited institutional curricula, inconsistent training standards, and cultural misconceptions about “soft skills.” The LSCDF developed through this research provides a structured model integrating cognitive, emotional, and behavioural domains to cultivate sustainable professional growth and psychological resilience.

The study concludes that life skills are not auxiliary attributes but core competencies for ethical and effective mental-health practice. The proposed framework offers practical pathways for educators, administrators, and policymakers to embed life-skills training within academic programmes, supervision systems, and institutional leadership development — aligning with the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Mental Health Action Plan (2013–2030) and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 3 (Good Health and Well-Being).

title: Strategic Leadership Models for Sustainable Mental Health Organisations

detail.title: Strategic Leadership Models for Sustainable Mental Health Organisations
detail.abstract: Mental-health organisations operate in complex and high-pressure environments where clinical excellence must coexist with financial accountability, ethical care, and workforce resilience. Sustainability in such settings depends not only on resource management but on strategic leadership models that integrate purpose, people, and policy. This doctoral thesis investigates strategic leadership for sustainable mental-health organisations, examining how leaders foster cultures of compassion, innovation, and coproduction while navigating systemic challenges such as workforce shortages, limited funding, and fragmented governance. Drawing on a narrative-synthesis methodology, it reviews empirical and theoretical studies from 2015-2025 covering transformational, authentic, adaptive, and distributed-leadership paradigms. Findings indicate that sustainability arises when leaders create psychologically safe workplaces, empower multidisciplinary teams, share decision-making power with service users, and align organisational practices with broader health-policy and equity agendas. The research introduces a Strategic Leadership Sustainability Framework (SLSF) linking three core domains-People, Process, and Policy-to show how leadership behaviours translate into long-term organisational resilience and equitable outcomes. The thesis concludes that sustainable mental-health leadership demands a shift from hierarchical command models toward collaborative, learning-oriented systems grounded in ethical accountability. Its recommendations provide actionable guidance for managers, policymakers, and educators seeking to build a next generation of leaders capable of shaping just, inclusive, and future-ready mental-health systems.

detail.abstract: This article examines strategic approaches for the European Union's Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA) to embed proportionality within its AML/CFT regulatory framework. It advocates for principles-based regulation complemented by supervisory convergence mechanisms, such as peer reviews and joint supervisory efforts, to foster mutual trust and prevent regulatory arbitrage across member states. The paper highlights the importance of establishing a regulatory maturation process that enables continuous, risk-aligned development of rules through iterative review and stakeholder engagement. Additionally, it emphasises the role of comprehensive cost-benefit analyses that consider proportionality and EU competitiveness, benchmarking against international standards. By integrating these strategies, AMLA can create a proportionate, effective, and adaptable regulatory environment that supports the EU’s broader economic and supervisory objectives, ensuring the effectiveness and competitiveness of its AML/CFT regime from its inception.

detail.abstract: This article explores the nature, origins, and enduring significance of hierarchy culture as one of the core organizational culture types within the Competing Values Framework. Defined by order, control, and predictability, hierarchy culture prioritizes stability, efficiency, and compliance over flexibility or innovation. Drawing from classical theories of bureaucracy by Weber, Taylor, and Fayol, and integrating insights from modern institutional and contingency theory, the article examines how hierarchical systems sustain legitimacy, scale, and accountability across diverse contexts-from the U.S. Army and McDonald's to Toyota and global financial institutions. It analyzes the characteristic structures, leadership behaviors and communication patterns that make hierarchy both a source of reliability and a potential barrier to adaptability. The discussion further explores how hierarchy evolves as organizations mature and the tensions it creates in balancing control with responsiveness. Ultimately, the article argues that hierarchy's survival depends on adaptive hybridization-preserving its discipline and legitimacy while integrating flexibility to meet the demands of a dynamic world.

This white paper further examines the structural disparities embedded within artificial intelligence systems, as revealed by the 7 Races of AI Framework (previously published February 2, 2025, on SSRN). Through an empirical analysis of AI knowledge-tiering, it demonstrates how AI models—despite being constructed on binary logic—continues to exhibit discriminatory information-gating practices, limiting knowledge accessibility based on economic privilege and human based system-level governance.

By analyzing discrepancies in free-tier versus paid-tier AI responses, this study establishes that AI is not merely a passive knowledge tool but an assumed regulated ecosystem where access to what is often promoted as unarguable truth is monetized and controlled. The paper then introduces a regionalized AI governance strategy, tailored for policymakers and industry leaders in different global regions, helping to ensure that AI remains an equitable digital entity rather than a controlled gatekeeping system.

title: People versus Places: Elite Persistence after the Fall of the Ming
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder - Department of Economics and University of Colorado

detail.title: People versus Places: Elite Persistence after the Fall of the Ming
detail.abstract: We study how elite power persisted through the Ming–Qing transition in Central China. Using genealogical microdata on married couples and their descendants, linked to measures of local elite influence, we estimate the effects of the Ming collapse (1368–1644) on families (people) and on regions (places). A family line-level treatment and control approach shows that elites experienced an immediate loss of influence, but their descendants recovered and consolidated elite status under the Qing (1644–1911). In contrast, a region-level design indicates that areas more heavily exposed to Ming-collapse destruction suffered persistent adverse outcomes. Evidence on career choice is consistent with a trauma-induced shift toward civil service examination careers, with stronger intergenerational transmission of exam-oriented norms in families more exposed to destruction. The results document adaptive persistence of elite families despite regime change, alongside lasting regional scarring, and highlight the role of cultural transmission in the persistence of elite status.
